strengths: SDCI addresses a meaningful limitation of fixed-graph relational inference: interactions can change with an object's state. The combination of state-conditioned graphs, amortized inference, and a shared dynamics decoder is intuitive and potentially useful.

The synthetic experiments measure recovery of ground-truth structure, states, and dynamics parameters, providing evidence beyond prediction accuracy. Reported test edge accuracy improves from 66.44% for ACD to 93.84% on observed-state linear data, and from 69.60% to 80.82% on hidden-state spring data.

The fixed-decoder experiments help distinguish graph-inference performance from dynamics fitting. The paper also reports the unsuccessful temporal architecture and examines increasing numbers of states. Architecture diagrams, training settings, and simulator equations make the main implementation understandable.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not establish an advantage over methods suited to changing interactions. ACD is the only baseline and assumes a fixed graph, making its disadvantage on switching graphs unsurprising. Comparisons with dynamic relational inference, regime-switching methods, and a simple state-conditioned VAR regression are needed. The related-work discussion also insufficiently positions the contribution against these alternatives, leaving its originality and practical significance uncertain.

The claimed coverage of hidden states determined by earlier events is not demonstrated clearly. Equation 20 estimates state from the current object's observation without a history model. The hidden linear state is simply the sign of the current value, and the hidden spring state depends on current position. The wall-collision experiment appears to use supervised state prediction and does not clearly establish recovery when the history-dependent state is withheld. This distinction materially limits the supported scope.

The causal interpretation of the learned decomposition needs stronger justification. The decoder receives states and observations, allowing changing behavior to be represented through decoder functions as well as edge selection. The stated Markov and no-confounding assumptions do not alone establish identifiability of jointly learned graphs, states, and mechanisms. Indeed, the spring experiments show similar reconstruction errors for substantially different graph accuracies. The paper should explain when its graph interpretation is warranted or narrow its claims to the demonstrated simulator settings.

The empirical evidence is narrow: both generators follow the assumed state-gating structure, use a prescribed number of states, and have only two edge types. Linear experiments contain just three variables and use a decoder matching the generating equation. Robustness to noise, larger graphs, and state-count misspecification is untested. The near-chance performance of the learned temporal variant and substantial train/test reconstruction gaps in Table 2 also warrant analysis before drawing broad reliability conclusions.

Important reproduction and evaluation details are missing, including dataset sizes, the spring-system particle count, repeated-run counts, and the meaning of the reported error bars. Hidden-state label-permutation handling and whether edge accuracy evaluates all state-conditioned graphs or only active edges are unspecified. The hidden-state encoder inputs and precise unsupervised training objective also need clarification. These omissions make the reported accuracies difficult to independently assess.

There are fixable but consequential mathematical specification errors. Equations 6 and 18 add log likelihood and positive KL divergence, which is neither the standard ELBO nor its negative; the prose instead describes minimizing negative log likelihood. The implemented objective should be stated consistently. Equation 21 also uses a weighted soft-edge relaxation rather than an exact categorical sample from Equation 19, and this approximation should be identified explicitly.

The synthetic experiments demonstrate substantial graph-recovery improvements over ACD: test accuracy increases from 66.44% to 93.84% on linear data and from 69.60% to 80.82% on springs with hidden, position-dependent states. Evaluating ground-truth edges alongside reconstruction error is appropriate.

weaknesses: The comparisons do not establish the contribution relative to methods that support changing graphs. Comparisons with dynamic relational inference, such as dNRI, and a simple state-conditioned or switching regression baseline would help establish whether the proposed combination offers a meaningful advance. Related work insufficiently addresses these alternatives.

The hidden linear state is an instantaneous threshold of the observed variable, and the hidden spring state depends on current position. Equation 20 likewise uses only current object variables. The wall-collision experiment predicts state transitions but does not clearly establish recovery when the history-dependent state is withheld. The causal interpretation requires stronger justification. The stated SCM, temporal-ordering, and Markov assumptions do not by themselves establish identification of both latent states and graph structure. Flexible message functions can ignore an active edge or implement state dependence internally, allowing different graph representations to explain the same dynamics. The paper should distinguish demonstrated simulator-edge recovery from general causal identification and specify additional conditions or supporting analyses.

The optimization description contains consequential ambiguities. Equations 6 and 18 add log-likelihood and KL divergence, which is neither the conventional maximized ELBO nor its minimized negative; the stated negative-log-likelihood supervision suggests a sign error. Equation 21 replaces categorical sampling with a weighted mixture without explaining how this enters Equation 12's discrete selector. strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: discovering interactions whose structure changes with an object's state. Reusing state-conditioned summary graphs provides an intuitive and practical extension of amortized causal discovery.

The synthetic experiments evaluate ground-truth graph recovery alongside reconstruction and parameter estimation. Reported improvements over ACD are substantial: linear-data test edge accuracy increases from 66.44% to 93.84%, while the location-dependent spring experiment improves from 69.60% to 80.82%.

The fixed-decoder controls help separate graph inference from dynamics learning, and the state-count sweep provides useful initial evidence about increasing difficulty. The paper reports the unsuccessful temporal architecture candidly and supplies several training and architecture details.
weaknesses: The causal interpretation has an unresolved ambiguity. In Eq. (12), message functions receive the state as part of their input, so an always-present edge can produce zero influence in a particular state through the message function itself. State-dependent effects can therefore be represented through either graph changes or decoder behavior. The stated SCM and Markov assumptions, together with a uniform edge prior, do not resolve this ambiguity. The paper needs to explain when its latent edges identify structural relationships rather than merely providing a useful predictive representation.

The comparison does not establish the contribution relative to methods that can represent changing interactions. ACD, the only experimental baseline, assumes a stationary graph and is consequently structurally disadvantaged. Comparisons with state-conditioned regression, switching models, or dynamic relational inference would be substantially more informative. The related-work discussion also overlooks relevant nonstationary and regime-dependent causal discovery approaches, leaving originality and significance insufficiently established.

The hidden-state formulation and its experimental coverage are incomplete. Eq. (20) infers states from current object quantities, which does not explain recovery of states requiring historical information. The clearly hidden-state experiments use instantaneous sign or position rules. The collision experiment should specify whether state labels are available during training and inference. Additionally, the manuscript does not clearly explain how the state-conditioned encoder and the state-likelihood term in Eq. (18) are trained when those labels are unavailable.

The evaluation provides a promising proof of concept but limited understanding of failure conditions. The linear experiment uses only three variables and a decoder matching the generator, and all experiments use two edge types. In Table 2, increasing the state count while holding sequence length at 80 reduces observations per state, confounding model difficulty with information availability. The learned SDCI-Temporal model's approximately chance-level accuracy also deserves a more substantive diagnosis.

Important reproducibility and statistical details are missing, including training/test sample counts, the number of independent runs, the meaning of the reported uncertainty intervals, the exact location-to-state rule for springs, and latent-state label alignment. Framewise state accuracy is also insufficient to establish successful transition detection without transition frequencies or a persistence baseline.

There are correctable mathematical and terminology issues. Eqs. (6) and (18) add log-likelihood and KL terms with the same sign, yielding neither the standard ELBO nor its negative; the actual optimized loss should be clarified. The manuscript also conflates invariant conditional dynamics with stochastic stationarity, despite explicitly using unstable linear processes.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful limitation of stationary graph inference. Conditioning interactions on the source object's state is an interpretable extension of amortized causal discovery, and sharing interaction functions across states is a sensible modeling choice.

The synthetic results provide substantive evidence that SDCI-Static recovers the simulated interactions. Test edge accuracy improves from 66.44% for ACD to 93.84% on the linear task, and from 69.60% to 80.82% on the hidden-state spring task. Recovering simple unobserved state partitions is a useful proof of concept.

The fixed-decoder comparisons help separate graph inference from dynamics learning, while the state-count sweep exposes performance degradation as complexity increases. Reporting the unsuccessful temporal architecture also provides useful information about the method's limitations.
weaknesses: The central comparison is insufficient to establish comparative significance. ACD is the only baseline and cannot represent changing graphs, so the results primarily demonstrate the benefit of adding the required representational capacity. Comparisons with switching or state-conditioned models, including a switching VAR on linear data and dynamic relational inference on springs, are needed. The related-work discussion also insufficiently addresses these relevant approaches.

The hidden-state evidence is narrower than the motivating scenarios suggest. The linear hidden state is exactly a threshold of the current observation, and the hidden spring state depends on current position. Equation 20 likewise infers states from current object observations without a history model. The wall-collision experiment appears to use supervised state prediction, so it does not establish recovery of unobserved history-dependent regimes. Section 4.1 also incorrectly classifies the instantaneous threshold example as scenario class 3.

The causal interpretation needs stronger justification. Assuming an SCM, first-order Markov dynamics, and no confounding does not establish that this flexible reconstruction objective uniquely recovers the graph and latent-state decomposition. The paper supplies neither sufficient identification conditions nor an analysis of alternative graph/state/decoder explanations. The observed graph recovery supports the specific simulators, but the boundary between predictive interaction learning and identifiable causal discovery remains unclear.

The optimization description contains consequential ambiguities. Equations 6 and 18 combine positive log-likelihood with positive KL divergence, which is inconsistent with either ELBO maximization or negative-ELBO minimization. This may be a correctable notation error, but the actual objective must be specified. Equation 21 also replaces the categorical sampling in Equation 19 with a weighted edge vector; this is an approximation whose integration with the decoder and hidden-state training loss is not adequately explained.

Robustness is insufficiently investigated even within the proposed setting. Experiments use binary edge types and simulator dynamics closely matched to the model; the linear decoder explicitly mirrors the generating equation and evaluation is restricted to three variables. SDCI-Temporal reaches only 49.97% test accuracy, while Table 2 shows substantial reconstruction generalization gaps, such as training MSE 0.0008 versus test MSE 0.0402 for two states. These failures deserve analysis and controlled tests of noise, system size, and regime coverage.

Important reproduction and reliability details are missing: dataset sizes, the number of independent runs, the meaning of the reported uncertainty values, latent-state label alignment for accuracy evaluation, and the precise position-based state rule. The test reconstruction horizon and teacher-forcing protocol are also unclear. These omissions make it difficult to assess the statistical reliability and reproduce the strongest results.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful limitation of fixed-graph time-series models. Representing changing interactions through source-node states and reusable state-specific graphs is an interpretable, well-motivated extension of amortized causal discovery.

The controlled experiments provide direct evidence of graph recovery under the proposed generative assumptions. On the two-state linear task, SDCI-Static achieves 93.84% test edge accuracy versus 66.44% for ACD, alongside substantially improved reconstruction and accurate recovery of interaction parameters.

The hidden-state experiments offer a promising proof of concept: reported test edge accuracies reach 91.96% on linear data and 80.82% on springs. The experiments varying the number of observed states also help characterize performance as the inference problem becomes harder.

The fixed-decoder comparisons help separate graph inference from dynamics learning. The paper also reports the unsuccessful temporal architecture, and provides useful optimizer, teacher-forcing, architecture, and simulator details.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not sufficiently establish the contribution relative to methods capable of changing graphs. ACD is the only baseline, and its fixed-graph restriction prevents it from representing the principal benchmarks. Comparisons with dynamic relational inference, switching dynamical models, and a state-conditioned linear estimator would help determine the benefit of the proposed inference approach. The related-work discussion also gives insufficient attention to these directly relevant alternatives.

The evidence for hidden states is substantially narrower than the introductory taxonomy suggests. The linear hidden state is a threshold of the current observation, and the hidden spring state depends on current position. Equation (20) likewise infers states from current object variables, without a history-dependent inference mechanism. The wall-collision experiment uses state-prediction supervision and does not establish unsupervised recovery of history-dependent hidden states. In particular, identifying the linear experiment as scenario class 3 is misleading.

The evaluation leaves robustness and practical scope uncertain. Both simulators use only two edge types; the linear task contains three variables and a decoder matching the generating equation. There are no meaningful tests of observation noise, graph-size scaling, or misspecified state counts. Important failures also remain unexplained: SDCI-Temporal achieves approximately chance edge accuracy with a learned decoder, and Table 2 reports a roughly fiftyfold train–test reconstruction gap for two states.

The causal interpretation needs a clearer justification. Assuming an SCM, first-order dynamics, and no latent confounders does not by itself establish identifiability of jointly learned states and graphs. The ground-truth graph evaluations support recovery in the tested simulator families, but the paper does not explain when alternative state/graph decompositions can be ruled out. Additionally, invariant dynamics within a state should be distinguished from distributional stationarity: the deliberately unstable linear simulator does not become stationary simply by fixing its state.

The training formulation is insufficiently precise, especially for hidden states. Equations (6) and (18) give log-likelihood and KL terms the same sign, which is inconsistent with the stated minimization objective; this may be a notation error, but the implemented loss must be clarified. More substantively, the paper does not clearly specify the encoder inputs and replacement for supervised state-loss terms when states are hidden, or how the soft edge mixture in Equation (21) is used with the categorical decoder formulation.

Several omissions prevent reliable reproduction and assessment of uncertainty: training/test sample counts, the number of independent runs, the meaning of the reported ± quantities, the spring-system particle count, and the exact position-based state rule are unspecified. Edge-accuracy aggregation and latent-state label alignment also need definitions. These details are particularly important for interpreting the reported near-perfect unsupervised state accuracies.

strengths: Conditional summary graphs are a useful contribution: under the assumption that outgoing effects depend on the source variable’s state, K graphs compactly represent K^N joint state configurations. This meaningfully extends approaches based on a single global regime.

The combination of shared interaction functions, amortized graph inference, and state-dependent message passing is well motivated. The paper clearly explains its relationship to NRI/ACD and distinguishes population identifiability from the unresolved consistency of its learning procedure.

The synthetic results demonstrate benefits within the proposed setting. For example, Table 2 reports 97.08% summary-graph accuracy versus ACD’s 60.45% for two edge types with hidden states. Experiments varying state counts, training-set sizes, and numbers of variables, together with NBA forecasting, provide useful breadth.
weaknesses: The central identifiability guarantee needs a more precise statement and proof. Theorem 1 omits the nonconstant-mechanism assumption used in Lemma 2. More importantly, Appendix A.3 invokes causal minimality to conclude dependence after conditioning on all other lagged variables, whereas minimality directly guarantees dependence only conditional on the other parents. That implication requires additional justification and suitable support/nondegeneracy assumptions. The result also concerns population identification, rather than recovery by the proposed VAE.

The comparisons do not adequately establish an advantage over methods designed for switching causal structures. Regime-PCMCI is identified as closely related but is not evaluated; most evaluated baselines assume fixed structures or smoothly changing mechanisms. Moreover, SDCI learns shared dynamics from 50,000 training sequences, while several competitors fit individual sequences. Comparisons with switching-regime methods and amortized dynamic-graph models are needed to isolate the proposed contribution.

The demonstrated hidden-state capability is substantially narrower than the introductory framing suggests. Appendix F.2 explicitly reports unsuccessful causal recovery with hidden history-dependent states and supplies state supervision for scenario class 3. Successful hidden-state experiments mainly use simple deterministic functions of current observations. This limitation should appear prominently in the main text. Performance also deteriorates substantially in the unrestricted three-edge-type setting, where Table 2 does not show a clear advantage over TdCM.

The graph-recovery evaluation is incomplete for the central claim about changing structures. In particular, the hidden-state spring comparison reports accuracy of the union summary graph, which discards when edges occur and can be dominated by edge prevalence. Actual graph densities, trivial prediction baselines, precision/recall, and quantitative conditional or full-time graph recovery would make these results more convincing.

NBA forecasting improvements support the usefulness of the model’s inductive bias, but do not establish that its learned interactions are causal. A comparable state-conditioned graph predictor without causal-structure discovery would help assess that interpretation. The rollout protocol also needs clarification about access to future ball features and state labels, and the train/test construction should establish separation between games and potentially overlapping events.

Reproduction and uncertainty assessment remain incomplete despite the implementation appendix. The manuscript does not clearly specify the graph-prior probabilities, hidden-state network architecture, latent-label alignment for accuracy calculations, or the number of training runs and meaning of the reported error bars. The unexplained lambda parameter in Appendix C.2 further obscures the training objective.

strengths: The variable-specific state formulation addresses a meaningful limitation of stationary and global-regime models. Under the assumption that outgoing interactions depend on the source variable’s state, conditional summary graphs compactly represent up to K^N joint configurations using K graphs. This is a useful conceptual extension of amortized causal discovery.

The state-conditioned graph VAE provides a coherent implementation with shared interaction functions and amortized inference across sequences. Synthetic results demonstrate substantial benefits in some settings: for binary hidden-state linear data, Table 2 reports 97.08% summary-graph accuracy and 98.08% conditional-summary-graph accuracy, versus 60.45% summary-graph accuracy for ACD.

The evaluation investigates several relevant dimensions, including variable and state counts, training-data size, fixed versus learned decoders, and transfer across system sizes and basketball teams. NBA forecasting improvements provide evidence of practical predictive value, while the appendices supply substantial architectural and simulation details.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not adequately establish the advantage over methods designed for discrete regime changes. Regime-PCMCI, identified as the closest related approach, is absent from the experiments. Several evaluated baselines are explicitly described as unsuitable for the simulated switching dynamics. Moreover, comparisons against methods fitted to individual sequences also incorporate SDCI’s access to 50,000 training sequences. Comparisons with switching models on feasible settings are needed to distinguish the proposed contribution from these advantages.

The principal quantitative hidden-state spring experiment evaluates the union summary graph, which discards the state dependence central to the paper’s objective. Union graphs can also be dense, making raw accuracy misleading without class proportions and trivial baselines. For example, two independently sampled 50%-dense state graphs yield a union on which predicting every edge achieves 75% expected accuracy. Conditional-graph or time-resolved edge metrics, precision/recall, and majority baselines are needed to establish reliable state-dependent recovery.

The identifiability theorem requires a more careful statement and proof. Theorem 1 does not explicitly include the nonconstant-parent-effect assumption used in Lemma 2. Appendix A.3 then infers dependence conditional on all other lagged variables from causal minimality, which establishes dependence conditional on the remaining parents; the stronger conclusion requires an additional argument and suitable support assumptions. Furthermore, identifiability of the ideal SCM does not establish recovery by the relaxed amortized VAE, a limitation acknowledged in Appendix A.3 but obscured by the abstract’s claim that the approach recovers dependencies 'provably.'

The advertised scope exceeds the demonstrated hidden-state capability. The introduction suggests coverage of scenario classes 1–3, but Appendix F.2 explicitly reports failure with hidden history-dependent states and instead supplies state information during training. The stated inference model q(s_i^t | x_i^t) also lacks the history needed for general scenario-class-3 inference. These claims should be narrowed or supported by an appropriate temporal state model and evaluation.

The NBA results establish predictive improvements but do not validate causal discovery or show that causal correctness explains those improvements. A capacity-matched, state-conditioned interaction model with fixed or fully connected graphs would help separate graph discovery from architectural benefits. The forecasting protocol also needs clarification about ball information available during the prediction horizon and how observed player states are obtained during rollout.

Several omissions limit reproducibility and confidence in the comparisons: the meaning of error bars and number of independent training runs are unspecified; state and edge-label permutation handling is unexplained; Appendix C.2 introduces an undefined lambda; and baseline thresholds and linear-data rejection criteria are not sufficiently specified. The latter also affect the graph distribution and state balance underlying the reported accuracies. Separately, Appendix D.1 incorrectly presents singular values below one as necessary for fixed-VAR stability; the relevant necessary-and-sufficient criterion is spectral radius below one.

Conditional summary graphs provide a useful, compact representation of changing interactions: under the source-state assumption, K graphs accommodate different states for individual variables without enumerating all K^N joint configurations.

SDCI is a coherent, well-motivated extension of amortized causal discovery, combining shared interaction functions, graph inference, and state-dependent edge selection. This combination has practical value even though much of the neural architecture follows ACD.

The experiments examine both fixed and sample-specific graphs, determined and recurrent states, simulated gene regulation, and NBA trajectories. Near-perfect fixed-graph recovery and the GRN F1 improvement from ACD's 0.187 to 0.347 provide promising evidence of practical value.

The graphical explanations are helpful, and the appendices provide substantial architecture, optimization, and simulation details. The paper also acknowledges difficulties with recurrent-state inference, selecting K, and establishing estimator consistency.
weaknesses: The central edge-type identifiability claim, Theorem 4.3/Corollary A.8, fails under the stated assumptions. These satisfy the derivative conditions in (a2) almost everywhere, yet both active message types contribute exactly x^2+2x. On a three-node ring where each node's states disable or enable its outgoing edge, active-edge assignments (1,1,2) and (1,2,2) therefore produce identical observation laws without being related by a global label permutation; (a1) still holds. Shared states couple outgoing messages, and nonlinear aggregation couples their contributions through the observation likelihood. Equation (56) does not correctly complete this marginalization. Moreover, setting q_s equal to p_s(s_t|x_t) generally excludes information supplied by future observations. This is a restricted variational approximation unless the gates are strictly deterministic.

Most graph baselines assume stationarity, while Appendix B.4 reports using default R-PCMCI settings after tuning encountered errors on short sequences. The GRN evaluation uses one bifurcating network, and its AUROC improvement over Rhino is only 0.936 versus 0.933 despite the much larger F1 difference. Table 1 lacks uncertainty estimates and an explicit threshold-selection protocol, making robustness and operating-point effects difficult to assess.

The application conclusions exceed the demonstrated scope. Recurrent inference with sample-specific graphs is evaluated only at three to five variables. The GRN experiment uses simulated longitudinal measurements of the same cells, which the appendix acknowledges are unavailable in ordinary sequencing experiments. NBA prediction conditions on ball features and supplies no causal ground truth. These results support the modeling approach but provide limited validation of causal correctness in realistic applications.

Several evaluation details needed for reproduction are missing: alignment of inferred state and edge-type permutations before scoring, the meaning of plotted error bars and number of training seeds, and the granularity of NBA train/test splits. strengths: Conditional summary graphs provide a useful, compact representation of source-state-dependent interactions, avoiding enumeration of K^N global regimes under the proposed factorization.

SDCI is a well-motivated extension of ACD and neural relational inference. Combining shared interaction functions with latent states accommodates structural changes both within sequences and across samples.

The empirical results show promise: near-perfect fixed-graph recovery on particle simulations, improved summary-graph recovery against the selected baselines, and GRN F1 of 0.347 compared with 0.187 for ACD.

The illustrations and implementation appendices help explain the approach. The paper appropriately acknowledges unresolved estimator consistency, selection of K, and difficulties with recurrent states.
weaknesses: The edge-label identifiability claim in Theorem 4.3 has a substantive counterexample. Corollary A.8 incorrectly concludes that permutation invariance makes aggregation derivatives equal across inputs and targets. Consider f0=0, f1(x,y)=x, f2(x,y)=π−x, and g({h_i})=Σ_i sin(h_i). These satisfy the stated derivative conditions almost everywhere, yet types 1 and 2 produce identical aggregated effects. Changing only some nonzero labels preserves the observation distribution without a global label permutation, while leaving distinct state-specific edge supports intact. Thus the stated assumptions do not establish edge-type identifiability.

The foundational mixture argument also needs repair. In Theorem A.6, Eqs. (34)–(35) use Gaussian-mixture identifiability to recover every regime and their number without assuming positive mixture weights. Deterministic states can leave only one active component at a given history, and unrestricted state dynamics permit regimes that never occur. Such regimes and their graphs cannot be identified. Additional support assumptions and a justified argument for the determined-state setting are necessary.

The exact-inference claim in Section 3.3 and Appendix B.2 is unsupported for the soft categorical implementation. Future observations generally update beliefs about states, so p(s_t|x_t) is not the full posterior. Shared states also couple their children after marginalization, and nonlinear aggregation prevents the general elementwise simplification in Eq. (56). Setting q=p can define a variational approximation, but does not establish the claimed O(NK) exact inference unless further restrictions, such as deterministic point-mass states, apply.

The experiments establish a narrower advantage than the broad superiority claims suggest. The particle comparisons primarily use methods with fixed graph structure; R-PCMCI is evaluated only on the GRN simulation, using default settings after fitting difficulties. Stronger comparisons against methods that infer changing structures are needed. Recurrent inference with graphs varying across samples is demonstrated only for three and five variables, leaving practical scalability in a central target setting unresolved.

The GRN evidence comes from one simulated 49-gene network, and its AUROC improvement over Rhino is only 0.936 versus 0.933. Table 1 lacks uncertainty estimates and a clear threshold-selection protocol, making the much larger F1 difference difficult to interpret. Appendix C.2 also acknowledges that the required same-cell longitudinal measurements are unavailable in standard sequencing experiments. NBA forecasting and qualitative visualizations demonstrate predictive usefulness but do not validate causal interpretations of the learned edges.

Reproduction and assessment of robustness would benefit from explicit run counts, definitions of plotted error bars, state/edge-label permutation matching for evaluation, and the NBA splitting protocol. The useful methodological contribution merits further development, but the central theoretical and inference issues require substantive revision before acceptance.

strengths: Conditional summary graphs provide a useful representation of changing causal structure. Under the outgoing-edge factorization, K graphs represent K^N joint state configurations. Combining this representation with ACD/NRI-style inference is a meaningful, well-motivated contribution.
The reported fixed-graph particle experiments show near-perfect structure recovery. The DynGen result also demonstrates practical promise, with F1 improving to 0.347 compared with 0.187 for ACD.

The source derivatives 0, 1, and -1 satisfy (a2.2), and the aggregation derivatives satisfy (a2.1) almost everywhere. Nevertheless, both nonzero types produce identical effects because sin(pi-x)=sin(x). On a three-node directed cycle with on/off source states, assumption (a1) holds, but active-edge labelings (1,1,2) and (1,2,2) produce identical observation laws without being related by one global label permutation. Corollary A.8 also incorrectly infers equal aggregation derivatives from permutation invariance. This undermines a principal theoretical contribution.

The regime-identifiability argument has a separate support gap. Theorem A.6 applies Gaussian-mixture identifiability in Eqs. (34)-(35) without ensuring positive component weights. For deterministic observation-dependent states, only one component is active at a given history; unrestricted state dynamics can also leave regimes unvisited. The cited mixture result therefore does not establish identification of every regime or the unknown number of states. Additional assumptions or a separate identification argument are required.

The claimed exact inference in Appendix B.2 is not established for the categorical model actually specified. Although p(s_t|x_t) describes state generation, the posterior given the complete trajectory generally also depends on successor observations. Furthermore, marginalizing a source state induces dependence among its children, which the element-wise factorization in Eq. (56) does not preserve. Setting q equal to the state generator can define a variational approximation, but it does not justify the claimed exact posterior inference or O(NK) exact marginalization.

The comparisons provide limited evidence against competing approaches that explicitly learn changing regimes. Particle experiments primarily compare against methods with fixed causal structure, while R-PCMCI appears only in the GRN experiment and uses defaults after tuning encountered short-sequence failures. Direct comparisons on conditional-graph recovery would better isolate the contribution. Figure 5 also shows substantial deterioration for sample-specific graphs, including recurrent systems with only three or five variables.

The biological evidence is restricted to one simulated 49-gene network. Table 1 reports nearly identical AUROC for SDCI and Rhino (0.936 versus 0.933), despite very different F1 scores, making the unspecified threshold-selection procedure consequential. Independent network replicates, seed variability, precision-recall evaluation, and explicit label-permutation matching would strengthen the conclusions and reproducibility. Appendix C.2 also acknowledges that the required longitudinal measurements of individual cells are unavailable in ordinary sequencing experiments, limiting the claimed direct applicability.

The NBA experiment supports conditional predictive usefulness, but cannot validate causal interpretations without ground-truth structure or interventions. The improvement over ACD is modest, and forecasts condition on ball features. The evaluation should explicitly document future ball-feature availability, game/event separation between splits, and uncertainty across training runs before drawing broader forecasting conclusions.

SDCI is a well-motivated extension of ACD/NRI, combining shared interaction functions with local latent states and supporting structures that vary across sequences. This combination constitutes a meaningful methodological contribution.

strengths: The conditional summary graph is a useful, well-motivated contribution. Under the sender-state dependence assumption, it represents interactions using K graph templates instead of enumerating K^N global regimes. Combining this representation with shared message functions provides a substantive extension of ACD/NRI.

The empirical results demonstrate practical promise: nearly perfect structure recovery in the fixed-graph particle experiments, improved GRN F1 (0.347 versus 0.187 for the strongest reported baseline), and better NBA forecasting than VRNN and NRI-NPM.

The evaluation distinguishes observed, determined, and recurrent states and considers graphs varying across samples. The manuscript acknowledges difficulties with recurrent inference and the absence of estimator consistency guarantees. Detailed architecture, training, and simulation descriptions, together with a code link, support reproduction.
weaknesses: Major theoretical issue: Theorem A.6 applies Gaussian-mixture identifiability in Eqs. (35)–(36) to identify all U components at each history, without ensuring their mixing weights are positive. In the deterministic-state setting, only one component may be active at a given history; unrestricted state dependencies can also make joint configurations inaccessible. Standard mixture identifiability therefore does not justify this step. A support/coverage argument and revised proof are needed before claiming identification of all regimes and the unknown number of states.

Major theoretical issue: Corollary A.8 asserts that permutation invariance of g makes its partial derivatives equal across senders and receivers, enabling a single global edge-type permutation. This is false for general permutation-invariant functions: g(h1,h2)=exp(h1)+exp(h2) has unequal partial derivatives at unequal inputs. Moreover, shared nonlinear functions can have derivatives that depend on states through their message inputs. Consequently, the central edge-label identifiability result in Theorem 4.3 is not established by the supplied argument.

Major inference issue: Appendix B.2 does not establish exact O(NK) state inference. A sender's latent state jointly controls multiple outgoing messages, so marginalizing it generally induces dependencies between receiving variables; the factorization in Eq. (57) loses those dependencies. For the nondegenerate categorical model in Eq. (14), p(s_t|x_t) also generally differs from the posterior conditioned on future observations. Setting q equal to this local distribution can define a variational approximation, but does not make inference exact. The recurrent-state KL expression additionally needs an expectation over the latent history.

SDCI's AUROC of 0.936 is almost identical to Rhino's 0.933, despite a large F1 difference, making threshold selection and precision–recall evaluation particularly relevant. These protocols, label-permutation alignment, and the meaning of plotted error bars are insufficiently specified. Particle comparisons largely use stationary baselines, while R-PCMCI is evaluated with default settings on short GRN sequences; stronger comparisons with methods designed for changing regimes would better isolate the contribution.

The application and model-selection conclusions exceed the evidence. The NBA improvement over ACD is modest, and forecasting accuracy or plausible graph visualizations do not validate causal relationships. The forecasting protocol should specify whether future ball features are supplied and whether training and test games are disjoint. Likewise, reconstruction-error elbows in two synthetic settings provide limited evidence for reliably selecting K. The biological conclusions should acknowledge that the simulated longitudinal measurements of individual cells are unavailable in standard sequencing experiments.

strengths: Conditional summary graphs provide a useful representation of changing interactions. Under the sender-state assumption, storing K graph structures instead of K^N global regimes offers a meaningful modeling advantage.

SDCI is a well-motivated extension of amortized causal discovery and neural relational inference. Combining shared interaction functions with local latent states accommodates structures that vary both over time and across samples.

The empirical results are promising in several settings: nearly perfect structural recovery for shared synthetic graphs, improved GRN F1 for the determined-state variant (0.347 versus ACD’s 0.187), and better NBA forecasting than VRNN and NRI-NPM.

The manuscript situates the approach within relevant prior work, provides substantial implementation and dataset details, and links experimental code. It also appropriately acknowledges that estimator consistency remains unproved and reports difficulties in the recurrent-state setting.
weaknesses: Major theoretical issue: Theorem A.6 applies Gaussian-mixture identifiability in Eq. (36) as though all U conditional components have positive weights. No supporting positivity or coverage assumption is stated. In the intended deterministic-state setting, only one component may have positive weight at a given history, so this argument does not establish U = U-hat. Under the literal assumptions, unused states with distinct structures can also be introduced without changing the observation distribution. A support-aware proof and explicit minimality conditions are needed before claiming identification of all regime graphs and the unknown K.

Major theoretical issue: Corollary A.8, supporting Theorem 4.3, incorrectly assumes that permutation invariance makes the aggregation derivatives equal across edges and receivers and independent of states. For example, the permitted symmetric aggregator g(H) = sum_r(h_r + h_r^3) has strictly nonzero derivatives 1 + 3h_r^2 that differ between messages. Even the implemented aggregation can have derivatives depending on the receiving node and state-dependent message sum. Consequently, Eqs. (46)–(49) do not establish a single global permutation of edge types. This undermines a principal identifiability claim and requires stronger assumptions or a different proof.

Major inference issue: Appendix B.2 does not establish the claimed exact O(NK) state inference for the nondegenerate softmax state model. Although p(s_t | x_1:t) can simplify to p(s_t | x_t), subsequent observations generally update the posterior over s_t. Moreover, nonlinear aggregation couples incoming states, and one sender’s state affects multiple receivers; the elementwise marginalization in Eq. (57) does not remove these dependencies. Setting q_s = p_s can define a restricted variational approximation, but it is not generally exact posterior inference. The distinction matters for both the likelihood calculation and the claimed computational advantage.

The connection between the guarantees and evaluated systems needs clarification. Assumption (a1) requires every variable’s states to have distinct outgoing supports, whereas Appendix C.2 includes 16 target genes that only receive interactions and therefore have identical empty outgoing supports. These experiments may demonstrate useful behavior outside the assumptions, but they cannot validate the stated guarantee for that setting. Likewise, the two reconstruction-error elbows in Figure 7 provide limited evidence for reliable recovery of an unknown number of states.

The comparisons do not convincingly establish superiority over competing methods for changing causal structures. Figure 6 mainly compares against methods with fixed graph structures. R-PCMCI is evaluated on individual short GRN trajectories with default hyperparameters and subsequent graph averaging, while SDCI pools trajectories. In Table 1, SDCI’s AUROC of 0.936 is nearly identical to Rhino’s 0.933 despite a large F1 difference. Comparable threshold-selection procedures and precision–recall results are needed to determine how much of that difference reflects improved structural recovery.

The strongest practical claims extend beyond the demonstrated evidence. Performance deteriorates substantially when recurrent states and sample-varying graphs occur together (Figure 5). The biological evaluation uses one simulated network configuration, and the NBA experiment provides conditional forecasting and qualitative graph interpretations without causal ground truth. Its small advantage over ACD does not isolate the contribution of causal structure from additional model flexibility. Broader simulations and a capacity-controlled dynamic interaction baseline would strengthen the empirical case.

Reporting omissions further limit assessment: the number of independent training runs and meaning of plotted error bars are unspecified, Table 1 lacks uncertainty estimates, and the procedure for aligning permutation-ambiguous state and edge labels is not explained. These are smaller concerns than the theoretical and inference issues, but they affect reproducibility and interpretation of the reported gains.

strengths: Conditional summary graphs offer a useful representation of changing causal structure. Under the sender-state assumption, representing K graphs instead of K^N global regimes provides a meaningful reduction in representational complexity.

SDCI is a well-motivated extension of ACD/NRI that combines shared interaction functions with learned local states. Supporting structures that change both within and across trajectories addresses an important limitation of stationary approaches.

The experiments demonstrate useful empirical behavior: almost perfect structure recovery in the shared-graph particle settings, and a substantial improvement in reported GRN F1, reaching 0.347 compared with 0.187 for the strongest baseline on that metric.
The manuscript provides extensive architecture, training, and dataset details and links to code. It also acknowledges unresolved estimator consistency and difficulties with recurrent-state inference.
weaknesses: Theorem 4.3 is false under the stated assumptions. Consider scalar variables with f0=0, f1(x,y)=x, f2(x,y)=pi-x, and g(y,{h})=sin(sum h). Use a three-node directed cycle, with each sender's two states enabling or disabling its outgoing edge. Assumptions (a1) and (a2) hold, including distinct interaction derivatives and nonzero aggregation derivatives almost everywhere. Nevertheless, both nonzero edge types produce sin(x). Assigning active edge labels (1,1,2) versus (1,2,2) around the cycle therefore gives identical transition distributions without a global label permutation, even with positive regime probabilities and independent Gaussian noise. Corollary A.8 incorrectly treats aggregation derivatives as independent of states and recipients; permutation invariance does not imply this. This directly undermines a principal theoretical contribution and requires stronger conditions and a revised proof.

Theorem A.6 has a separate gap at Eqs. (35)-(36). Pointwise Gaussian-mixture identifiability identifies components with positive conditional mixing weights. In the determined-state setting, only one regime has positive weight at a given history, so the asserted pointwise identification of all U regimes does not follow. The assumptions also do not explicitly exclude unused regimes. A regime-coverage condition and an argument accommodating different state supports are needed to support the graph-identifiability and unknown-K claims.

The exact-inference claim in Appendix B.2 is not justified for the specified stochastic softmax state model. Future observations inform earlier states, and the observation likelihood couples states through aggregation and shared children. Consequently, setting q(s_t|x_t)=p(s_t|x_t) does not generally recover the posterior given the full trajectory. Eq. (57) leaves message variables unmarginalized and does not establish O(NK) exact marginalization. Truly deterministic states would be a different case. The recurrent ELBO also needs an expectation over preceding latent states in its conditional KL terms. These distinctions matter for the claimed computational guarantees and interpretation of the training objective.

The comparative evaluation does not sufficiently resolve the empirical advantage of the central extensions. Particle comparisons primarily use baselines with stationary graphs within trajectories, while the recurrent setting lacks a competitive switching-model comparison. In Table 1, SDCI and Rhino have nearly identical AUROC values, 0.936 and 0.933, despite very different F1 scores. Threshold-selection details, precision-recall analysis, and uncertainty across training runs are needed to assess this difference. Regime-PCMCI is included on GRNs, but its reported short-sequence training difficulties weaken that comparison.

The application evidence supports narrower conclusions than some of the discussion suggests. GRN evaluation uses one simulated 49-gene network and longitudinal cell measurements unavailable in conventional sequencing experiments, limiting the claim of direct biological applicability. NBA results demonstrate conditional prediction given ball features; the improvement over ACD is modest, and there is no causal ground truth. The qualitative basketball interpretations therefore provide limited validation of causal recovery.
